problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A retailer forecasts weekly demand for 400 stores and 30,000 products, covering the next eight weeks. The forecast is due to replenishment by Monday 06:00; nightly sales data, promotions, and public holidays feed the process. Three data scientists own the pipeline, while central IT controls an unchanged data warehouse.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

points.description: A versioned data repository feeds scheduled, batch-based machine-learning pipelines orchestrated by an ML platform, with CI/CD automatically provisioning environments and building, testing, and deploying pipeline components. Trained model quality is tested, predictions are generated in scheduled batches and written to storage, and production data and predictions are logged and monitored.

Data is versioned in the code repository and processed in scheduled batch pipeline runs. CI/CD automatically provisions environments and builds, evidence-tests, and deploys models and system components; predictions are precomputed for reports, while production performance is monitored and prior model versions can be redeployed and restored when necessary.

Data is versioned in the code repository and processed in scheduled batch runs, with CI/CD building and testing pipeline components and trained-model quality before deployment. Models are served through precomputed forecasts or reports, while production data and predictions are monitored; if necessary, the system rolls back by redeploying and switching to a previous model version. Deployment automation is carried out through build and deployment scripts.

The system versions data in a dedicated data-version repository and uses CI/CD to build, test—including trained-model quality—and deploy the batch pipelines and components required for scheduled orchestrator runs, with environments provisioned automatically. Models produce precomputed predictions or forecasts for delivery as reports, while system data and predictions are logged and monitored in production.

Data is versioned in the code repository and processed in scheduled batch runs, with CI/CD automatically provisioning environments, running system integration tests, and deploying models and related components. Predictions are precomputed and delivered as reports; production model performance is monitored, with rollback to a previous model version available when needed.

Data is versioned in the code repository and processed in scheduled batch runs, with CI/CD building and testing pipeline components and trained-model quality before deployment. Models are served through precomputed forecasts or reports, with production data and predictions monitored; previous models can be redeployed for rollback, while environments are automatically provisioned and deployments are performed through manually invoked automation scripts.

The system versions data in a dedicated repository and triggers an orchestrated, batch-based ML pipeline when new training data becomes available; CI/CD automatically provisions environments and builds, tests—including trained-model quality—and deploys the required pipelines and components. Predictions are precomputed and delivered as reports, while data and predictions are logged and monitored, with the ability to redeploy and switch back to a previous model version.

Data is versioned in the code repository, while a scheduled batch pipeline periodically trains or processes data and precomputes predictions for delivery as reports. CI/CD automatically provisions environments and builds, tests model quality, and deploys models and components; production performance is monitored, with rollback to a previous model version available if needed.

Data is versioned in a code repository and processed through batch pipelines triggered on a schedule, with CI/CD building, integration-testing, and deploying the pipelines and their run-time components via deployment scripts. Models are precomputed for report-based serving, while system data and predictions are logged and monitored; a previous model can be redeployed for rollback, with development performed in an IDE.

The system versions data in a dedicated repository and uses automated provisioning to run scheduled, batch-based machine-learning pipelines orchestrated across their components. CI/CD builds, integration-tests, and deploys the pipelines and required components; scheduled batch serving writes predictions to storage while monitoring logs system data and predictions in production.

The system versions data in a dedicated repository, directly accesses the data provider, and uses automated provisioning to run scheduled batch pipelines orchestrated through an ML platform. CI/CD builds, tests, and deploys the pipelines and components, including trained-model quality tests; scheduled batch serving writes predictions to storage while data and predictions are logged and monitored.

approaches.idea: What if a dedicated data version repository and an orchestrator anchor a fully scheduled batch forecast pipeline?
What if code-based data versioning, evidence testing, and automated model delivery keep model experimentation fast?
What if a small team uses deployment scripts and an IDE to retain a simpler, partly manual operating model?
What if arrival of new training data triggers an orchestrated batch run with versioned inputs and rollback?

trajectory.hypothesis: A scheduled batch flow with versioned data and an orchestrator should fit R1 and C2; testing model quality should partly support R3/Q2 and logging should partly support Q3.
trajectory.observation: The point check is clean and no source attests the combination. Scheduled batch serving fits forecast delivery, while data versioning and automated environment provisioning help replay and maintainability; the six-hour runtime and warehouse access contract remain unproven.

trajectory.hypothesis: Code-repository data versioning plus evidence-based tests and automated delivery should support R2/R3 and Q1/Q2, while scheduled precomputation serves R1.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and the combination is unattested. Evidence-based testing and CI/CD support candidate comparison and release speed; the data-versioning choice does not capture model/environment versions, and performance monitoring does not guarantee failure alerts or atomic publication.

trajectory.hypothesis: A script-driven batch workflow should be maintainable with a small team while preserving model quality checks, historical data versions, and rollback.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and unattested. The simpler scripts may suit the small team, but manual deployment weakens the one-week release goal; choosing an IDE alone does not ensure a new member can recreate the environment.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace direct batch writes with precomputed forecast delivery to make the weekly replenishment handoff more explicit while retaining the reproducibility and orchestration choices.
trajectory.observation: The point check is clean and unattested. Precompute serving describes forecast/report delivery directly; the six-hour run limit and complete-publication guarantee still need implementation details absent from the space.

trajectory.hypothesis: Use system integration testing to check the deployed model and components as a whole, improving release confidence alongside the original evidence-based comparison.
trajectory.observation: The corrected point check is clean and unattested. Integration testing contributes deployment confidence but is less directly tied to comparing a candidate against the production model on past weeks than evidence-based hypothesis testing.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add automated environment provisioning to the script-based approach to improve Q4 while retaining the small-team operational model.
trajectory.observation: The point check is clean and unattested. Provisioning helps standardize environments, but the deployment scripts still require manual execution and the IDE choice does not guarantee full local reproducibility.

trajectory.hypothesis: Test whether a new-data trigger can start the orchestrated batch forecast with versioned inputs, quality tests, and rollback while reducing reliance on a fixed schedule.
trajectory.observation: The point check is clean and unattested. New-data triggering could start work when the warehouse load is ready, but it does not guarantee a weekly Monday deadline; the later refinement returns to a scheduled trigger and tests a controlled automated release path.

trajectory.hypothesis: Swap evidence-based hypothesis testing for explicit trained-model quality testing to ensure model quality is evaluated before automated release.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and unattested. Trained-model quality testing directly checks output quality but no longer explicitly represents comparison with the incumbent on past weeks, so the seed remains a stronger R3 fit.

trajectory.hypothesis: Use pipeline-component integration testing instead of trained-model quality testing to strengthen confidence that the scheduled workflow works end to end.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and unattested. Integration testing strengthens workflow confidence, but manual script deployment and the lack of an explicit model-quality test leave Q2 weaker than the seed's validation path.

trajectory.hypothesis: Shift the exploratory orchestrator design to CI/CD-driven model releases, retain rollback, and add system integration tests for safer automated deployment.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and unattested. CI/CD, integration tests, and rollback make a coherent release path; integration testing alone does not establish that a candidate beats the production model, and data versioning in code remains an incomplete replay record.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace the model-quality test with integration testing and use scheduled batch serving to write forecasts to storage, improving the delivery path for R1.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and unattested. Batch serving makes the storage handoff explicit, but integration testing is less direct for R3/Q2 than trained-model quality testing, so this does not improve the approach's best point.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add direct access to the existing data provider to make the warehouse boundary explicit while retaining the stronger quality-test and orchestration choices.
trajectory.observation: The check is clean and unattested. Direct provider access is the closest available match for leaving the warehouse in place, but the value does not specify read-only access or a controlled interface; this is an approximate fit.

adrs.title: Version historical data for replay
adrs.context: The team needs to reproduce forecasts from up to two years earlier. Data versioning supports replay, but the decision space does not include a full snapshot of model code, artifacts, libraries, and runtime state. Both choices are approximate fits to exact reproducibility.

pros: Separates data history from application code.
Supports keeping historical input versions.
cons: Adds a repository/tooling concern for a three-person team.
Does not capture model and runtime versions.
options.reason: Chosen in the orchestrated alternative for an explicit data-history boundary.

options.name: Version data in the code repository
pros: Keeps data version references near model and pipeline code.
cons: May be awkward for large or frequently changing datasets.
Still does not capture the complete execution state.
options.reason: Chosen by the other alternatives to keep versioning close to the team’s code workflow.

adrs.title: Run and deliver the weekly forecast as a batch
adrs.context: The workload is a weekly eight-week forecast that follows nightly loads and has a fixed Monday deadline. Batch processing and precomputation align with this cadence, but no value guarantees that 400 by 30,000 forecasts complete within six hours or defines an atomic replenishment handoff.

The space has no value guaranteeing a 15-minute failure alert, atomic publication, or a complete local environment.
